docs.snippet: The newswomen Katty Kay and Claire Shipman’s new book, “The Confidence Code,” aims to make women more self-assured.
docs.lead_paragraph: Katty Kay and Claire Shipman hardly seem like victims of self-doubt. Between them, they have covered the Clinton White House and the fall of the Soviet Union (Ms. Shipman), anchors BBC World News America (Ms. Kay) and learned to kiteboard at nearly 40 (Ms. Kay again). And yet both say they have had to work to overcome fears of inadequacy, tendencies to defer to male colleagues and “tortured cycles of useless self-recrimination.” In “The Confidence Code,” to be published on Tuesday, they lay out a path for women to become more self-assured. In phone conversations and at a lunch date (served by Sidra Forman, a Washington chef), Ms. Kay and Ms. Shipman discussed how to swat away creeping negative thoughts and what they are really thinking when they’re on television. docs.abstract: In our spring design issue, T celebrates risk takers, visiting the elegantly spare apartment of the architect Joseph Dirand, the amazing, overstuffed homes of Tangier’s eccentric expats and much more.
docs.snippet: In our spring design issue, T celebrates risk takers, visiting the elegantly spare apartment of the architect Joseph Dirand, the amazing, overstuffed homes of Tangier’s eccentric expats and much more.
docs.lead_paragraph: In our spring design issue, T celebrates risk takers. Leading the way is the architect-of-the-moment Joseph Dirand, whose elegantly spare Paris apartment, with its towering windows and generous slabs of marble, puts a new spin on minimalism. We travel to Tangier — long a refuge for adventurers and free-thinking outsiders — where a merry band of eccentric expats are letting their freak flags fly. We step into the homes of a pair of visionaries: the self-taught sculptor Alma Allen, whose journey as an art star has taken him from the streets of SoHo to the wild borderland of Joshua Tree, Calif., and the madcap designer Nicky Haslam, whose new London flat reflects his flair for the unconventional, and must be seen to be believed. Elsewhere, David Netto makes the case for personality and practicality in interior design; the international art gallery Hauser & Wirth bucks convention by opening an outpost in English farm country; the legendary French fabric house Le Manach gets a new lease on life; and the surrealist director Alejandro Jodorowsky as well as the surprisingly-nimble-in-the-kitchen pop star Kelis snack on gold popcorn while considering the future and blinged-out Louboutins. See all stories from the issue >>

(Showtime) DJANGO UNCHAINED (2012) Dr. King Schultz (Christoph Waltz), a German bounty hunter, teams up with Django (Jamie Foxx, above right, with Mr. Waltz), a former slave turned gun for hire, to rescue his wife (Kerry Washington) from a plantation owner (Leonardo DiCaprio) in this action-adventure directed by Quentin Tarantino. Samuel L. Jackson plays a house slave who assists his master. Writing in The New York Times, A. O. Scott called this film, which also earned Mr. Tarantino an Oscar for best original screenplay, “crazily entertaining, brazenly irresponsible and also ethically serious in a way that is entirely consistent with its playfulness.” He added: “Mr. Tarantino is a virtuoso of bloodshed, that is for sure, and also more enamored of a particularly toxic racial slur than any decent white man should be. But decency in the conventional sense is not his concern, though in another sense it very much is. When you wipe away the blood and the anarchic humor, what you see in ‘Django Unchained’ is moral disgust with slavery, instinctive sympathy for the underdog and an affirmation (in the relationship between Django and Schultz) of what used to be called brotherhood.”

docs.abstract: “Captain America: The Winter Soldier” was No. 1 movie in North America for the second weekend in a row, taking in an estimated $41.4 million.
docs.snippet: “Captain America: The Winter Soldier” was No. 1 movie in North America for the second weekend in a row, taking in an estimated $41.4 million.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Rio 2” got its wings a bit clipped at the weekend box office by a still-speeding superhero, while Kevin Costner was humiliated by a micro-budgeted horror flick. “Captain America: The Winter Soldier” (Walt Disney Studios) was the No. 1 movie in North America for the second weekend in a row, taking in an estimated $41.4 million, for a two-week domestic total of $159 million, according to Rentrak, which compiles ticketing data. “Rio 2” (20th Century Fox), an animated avian musical, was close behind with a solid $39 million, on par with the opening-weekend total for its series predecessor. But analysts and Fox, which backed “Rio 2” with a sizzling social media marketing campaign, had been predicting slightly higher totals. “Excellent weather across the middle of the country and the Northeast suppressed grosses in general yesterday and especially for matinees,” Chris Aronson, Fox’s president of domestic distribution, wrote in an email on Sunday morning. “Rio 2” has unusually light animated competition in the weeks ahead, Mr. Aronson noted.

headline.main: Cartoon Birds Can’t Stop Captain America

docs.lead_paragraph: Jennifer Lopez and Norman Lear were among those honored at the 25th annual Glaad Media Awards presented on Saturday in Los Angeles by the group formerly known as the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation. Ms. Lopez was given the Vanguard Award in recognition of her efforts to increase the visibility and understanding of gays, lesbians, bisexuals and the transgendered. She is also an executive producer on the ABC Family series “The Fosters,” which focuses on a lesbian couple and their children and was named outstanding drama series. Mr. Lear, who produced television series like “All in the Family” and “The Jeffersons” was the recipient of the Pioneer Award. The actress and transgender activist Laverne Cox received the Stephen F. Kolzak Award for her work in the Netflix series “Orange Is the New Black.” Other honorees included the Canadian pop duo Tegan and Sara for their album “Heartthrob”; the comic book series Young Avengers, by Kieron Gillen, Jamie McKelvie and Mike Norton from Marvel Comics; and Fuse’s reality series “Big Freedia: Queen of Bounce.” More awards are to be presented on May 3 at a ceremony in New York City.

docs.lead_paragraph: The choreographer Heidi Latsky has been selected as the first participant in a new short film series focusing on dance and choreography. The project, Dance for Film on Location at Montclair State University, in New Jersey, will be underwritten by a $450,000 grant from the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation and is to include three films by three different choreographers. The other two participants will be named later. Each work will be shown along with a live repertory that will become part of Peak Performances at Montclair State. In a statement, Jedediah Wheeler, the executive director of Peak Performances, said that the project is designed so that “the camera will not be used as a tool to document a performance, but rather as a collaborator to create a dance especially for film.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Conan O’Brien has joined the choir of late night television hosts who have praised CBS’s decision to name Stephen Colbert as the successor to David Letterman on “Late Show.” Mr. O’Brien told The Associated Press on Friday while backstage at a rehearsal for the MTV Movie Awards that Mr. Colbert is “fantastic,” and that he was looking forward to his work on “Late Show.” “I’m glad that it’s the right person getting it,” he said. Jimmy Fallon, the host of “The Tonight Show” on NBC, and Jimmy Kimmel, the host of his own show on ABC, had already voiced their approval of Mr. Colbert’s appointment. Mr. O’Brien, who hosted “The Tonight Show” for seven months before he was replaced by Jay Leno in 2010, denied any speculation that he had been a candidate for the “Late Show” appointment. “I wasn’t up for it,” Mr. O’Brien said and added that he was happy with his show, “Conan,” on TBS, which was renewed last year through November 2015. “I get to do what I want,” he said.

docs.abstract: Questions remain over whether vulnerable areas of California and the Pacific Northwest are adequately prepared for the Big One.
docs.snippet: Questions remain over whether vulnerable areas of California and the Pacific Northwest are adequately prepared for the Big One.
docs.lead_paragraph: It is hard to imagine any people, collectively, being better prepared for earthquakes than the Japanese. Their country is one long seismic zone, which at any moment could, literally, rock and roll. Every Sept. 1, across the archipelago, Japanese engage in exercises devoted to disaster awareness: what to do should the worst happen. The occasion resonates with history. On that date in 1923, the Great Kanto earthquake devastated Tokyo and nearby Yokohama, unleashing fire and fury that left more than 100,000 people dead. After that, Japan resolved that it would prepare for whatever cataclysm nature might throw at it.

headline.main: Promises of Preparedness Followed Devastating Earthquakes. And Yet.

(13) THE TRIALS OF MUHAMMAD ALI (2013) In 1967 — after changing his name from Cassius Clay, joining the Nation of Islam and refusing to be inducted into the United States military because of his religious opposition to the Vietnam War — Muhammad Ali, above, was convicted of draft evasion. Stripped of his world heavyweight championship and banned from boxing, he spent the next four years fighting legal battles. In 1971, his case for being a conscientious objector reached the United States Supreme Court. In this “Independent Lens” presentation, the director Bill Siegel combines interviews with Louis Farrakhan; Mr. Ali’s second wife, Khalilah Camacho-Ali; the journalist Robert Lipsyte; Mr. Ali’s loyal brother, Rahman; and a clerk from the Supreme Court proceedings to address Mr. Ali’s challenges then and now, including his battle with Parkinson’s. “The film falls short of explaining Mr. Ali, who, like many outspoken individuals, can stubbornly repel scrutiny, nor will it pacify the many who opposed his conscientious objections,” Nicolas Rapold wrote in The New York Times. “But it also underlines one enduring quality: namely, that he probably couldn’t care less what people think.”

docs.snippet: This is a simple yet addictive mix of salted cabbage and puréed avocado.
docs.lead_paragraph: Coleslaw meets guacamole here in this utterly simple mix of shredded cabbage, salt, lemon, and puréed avocado. The chef Iliana de la Vega, who was born in Oaxaca, Mexico, served it at a delicious Latin-themed lunch she prepared at the “Healthy Kitchens, Healthy Lives” conference this year at the Culinary Institute of America in Napa Valley. I couldn’t get enough of it. I sat with Iliana at the lunch and asked her about the salad. “Just salt the cabbage, let it sit for a while, then add lots of lemon juice and the mashed avocado,” she said. That really is all there is to it. Shred the cabbage thin and for best results let it sit, after salting generously, for an hour or more, to tenderize it and draw out strong-tasting juices.

headline.main: Chilean Cabbage and Avocado Slaw

docs.abstract: A salsa with a balance of char, heat, acid and creamy, based on a recipe by Kim Sunée.
docs.snippet: A salsa with a balance of char, heat, acid and creamy, based on a recipe by Kim Sunée.
docs.lead_paragraph: One of my favorite new cookbooks of this season is “A Mouthful of Stars” (Andrews McMeel), by Kim Sunée. The book is a memoir, travelogue and cookbook all rolled into one, written by an author who earlier published another compelling memoir with recipes,“Trail of Crumbs.” Kim is a poetic world traveler who loves many cuisines. She is a big fan of taco trucks and loves salsa, the spicier the better. This salsa is based on her recipe for roasted tomatillo-poblano salsa. I love its balance of char, heat, acid and creamy. I’m a moderate when it comes to heat, but you can make this hotter by adding more chiles.

headline.main: Roasted Tomatillo-Poblano-Avocado Salsa

docs.abstract: This salsa is closer to a salad, with a fusion of Thai and Mexican flavors.
docs.snippet: This salsa is closer to a salad, with a fusion of Thai and Mexican flavors.
docs.lead_paragraph: This is based on a recipe in Kim Sunée’s wonderful new book, “A Mouthful of Stars” (Andrews McMeel). Her recipe is more of a salad, a fusion of Thai and Mexican flavors. I loved the idea of combining avocado and papaya, two subtle, creamy fruits, with crunchy, bright-tasting Asian pears and spicy chiles. The first time I saw the recipe I wanted to test it right away, but I didn’t have Asian pears. So I used an apple, and loved it. It’s the sweet, crunchy fruit that does the trick, and apples and Asian pears both work. There are onions in the original recipe but I’ve made them optional.

headline.main: Chunky Avocado-Papaya Salsa

docs.abstract: Roasting the tomatillos produces a salsa with a deliciously charred flavor.
docs.snippet: Roasting the tomatillos produces a salsa with a deliciously charred flavor.
docs.lead_paragraph: I have been making tomatillo and avocado salsa for years, but I usually simmer the tomatillos rather than roasting them. Roasting the tomatillos, chiles and garlic – toasting really, as I use a skillet for this, on top of the flame – produces a salsa with a delicious charred flavor. I learned something recently from the chef Iliana de la Vega, who demonstrated the recipe at the “Healthy Kitchens, Healthy Lives” conference in Napa Valley in March: she says, in no uncertain terms, that you should not add water to tomatillo salsas. Without the water, this is a more intense salsa with pleasing density. You can use it as a sauce to serve with chicken or fish, or as a dip with chips or other vegetables.

headline.main: Avocado and Roasted Tomatillo Salsa

docs.abstract: The White House is sent a fresh pitch for a push to restore monarch butterfly habitat and food on public and private lands.
docs.snippet: The White House is sent a fresh pitch for a push to restore monarch butterfly habitat and food on public and private lands.
docs.lead_paragraph: All too often, species that humans care about only get attention when they are in crisis. Such is the case with monarch butterflies. The insect, famed for its remarkable annual migrations, faced declines in habitat on both the Mexican and American ends of its range for decades, but now is the focus of an urgent push for a rescue. The latest step is a letter sent on Monday to President Obama and relevant cabinet members by a group of scientists, educators, farmers, and other concerned citizens organized by the Xerces Society and other conservation groups focused on these butterflies. The letter (read it here) describes policies the administration could pursue on both public and private land along the butterfly’s migratory path.  In February, after about 20 naturalists, poets and other monarch defenders pressed for international action in an open letter, the plight of the butterfly was addressed by President Obama and his Mexican and Canadian counterparts at a summit. The leaders agreed to create a working group to study ways to protect the butterfly at both ends of its range. A recent article by Richard Conniff in Yale Environment 360 describes what farmers can do to help monarchs. I also recommend a recent feature in The Times by Michael Wines describing efforts by various groups to restore habitat:

docs.lead_paragraph: Last Thursday, in the middle of Salone del Mobile, Rossana Orlandi hosted a cocktail party at the Bagatti Valsecchi Museum. Champagne flowed as the see-and-be-seen crowd piled in to admire the “Untold” exhibition she curated there, which she explains in the above video interview with our design editor, Tom Delavan. Displaying contemporary pieces in the historic 19th-century house allowed Orlandi to “show how modern pieces are perfect and can have a fabulous dialogue with an old palace,” she says. The video opens with the light installation that she and Vionnet’s creative director, Goga Ashkenazi, commissioned from the artist Jacopo Foggini for the show. Orlandi, who was once a fashion designer and loathes the “trendsetter” label often tacked onto her globally-recognized name, is now famous for championing the careers of designers on the rise, a category Foggini fell into not long ago. “When I find a designer, first of all I want to be sure that this designer — he will grow up,” she explains. Cast in the fashion house’s signature shade of blue, Foggini’s installation set the tone for the queen of design’s fête — a high point during an action-packed week.

docs.lead_paragraph: Family is the North Star for Mona Simpson’s characters: It defines who they are, chaperones their choices, shapes their views of the world. Her dazzling debut novel, “Anywhere But Here” (1986), gave us an indelible portrait of a girl’s emotionally fraught relationship with her impossible, narcissistic mother. “The Lost Father” (1992) followed that same heroine’s obsessive search for the father who abandoned her. And “A Regular Guy” (1996) depicted another abandoned daughter trying to come to terms with her father — in this case, a rich, eccentric entrepreneur (who bore more than a passing resemblance to Ms. Simpson’s real-life brother, Steve Jobs).

docs.abstract: No, the absence of ‘Goths’ in bookstores is no great hole in the world.
docs.snippet: No, the absence of ‘Goths’ in bookstores is no great hole in the world.
docs.lead_paragraph: Seventeen years ago I wrote a book, which you can find on Amazon and Google and elsewhere online. This is unusual only because my book was never published. It’s called “Goths,” fitting for a title that has left its traces on the Internet but does not exist. The traces themselves are ghostly. Other than the title, Amazon lists only the publisher (Random House Trade), language (English) and ISBNs (one with 10 digits, the other with 13). Google goes further by giving the publication date (March 1, 1998) and promising a cover image — but it turns out to be a placeholder. And unlike Amazon, Google neglects to mention that the book is a hardcover. Google admits, “We haven’t found any reviews in the usual places,” which in this case would be the planet Earth. “Be the first to review this item,” Amazon encourages, but has as yet found no takers.

headline.main: The Book That Didn’t Exist

The deputy foreign minister for European-American affairs, Majid Takht-e Ravanchi, was quoted by the official Islamic Republic News Agency as saying that Iran had asked the Committee on Relations with the Host Country to examine the issue and that Secretary General Ban Ki-moon should intervene if necessary. But United Nations officials said that neither Mr. Ban’s office nor the committee had yet received any written complaint from Tehran or its United Nations mission. An official at the mission of Cyprus, which currently leads the committee, said that after it received a written complaint it could take up the issue at its next, yet-to-be-scheduled quarterly meeting. docs.abstract: Murders in Mexico declined in 2013, and they decreased significantly in several cities near the border with the United States, according to a new report.
docs.snippet: Murders in Mexico declined in 2013, and they decreased significantly in several cities near the border with the United States, according to a new report.
docs.lead_paragraph: Murders in Mexico declined in 2013, and they decreased significantly in several cities near the border with the United States, according to a new report from the Justice in Mexico Project at the University of San Diego to be released Tuesday. Using preliminary police data, researchers identified a homicide decrease of about 16 percent, with some of the biggest drops in murders in Ciudad Juárez and Monterrey, notoriously dangerous cities that have recently calmed down as the war between criminal gangs and the government has declined in intensity. Still, experts warn, it is not clear whether the decline is attributable to an overall weakening of organized crime: The number of gun-related murders has held steady as other kinds of killing have declined, and homicides have sharply risen in states farther south. Extortion and kidnapping have also increased nationwide. But with overall murder rates down for the second year in a row from their 2011 peak, some parts of Mexico appear to be on the mend, said David A. Shirk, an author of the report. “The decrease in violence that the government in Mexico is trying to convince people of is in fact real,” he said.

headline.main: Mexico: Homicides Decline Near Border, Report Says

docs.abstract: T’s design editor rounds up his favorites from this year’s Salone del Mobile.
docs.snippet: T’s design editor rounds up his favorites from this year’s Salone del Mobile.
docs.lead_paragraph: Salone del Mobile, Milan’s annual design week, concluded Sunday. As is custom, the official Salone event — where the biggest furniture companies introduce their latest designs all under one roof, in one of the largest convention centers in the world — was punctuated with a series of special exhibitions called Fourisalone (meaning “outside salone”), put on by local showrooms, shops and museums. And this year, a few underlying themes unified the whole experience. For starters, everyone, it seems, played up the contrast between new and current designs against the historic backdrop of the city. At the center of it all was Rossana Orlandi’s much-talked-about exhibition of contemporary works at the Museo Bagatti Valsecchi, a 19th-century palazzo. “I wanted to create a dialogue between the new and the old,” Orlandi said about the show, “Untold.”

headline.main: The Collections | The Top 10 Moments at Milan Design Week

docs.lead_paragraph: The photographer Leslie Williamson’s new book, “Modern Originals: At Home With Midcentury European Designers,” out from Rizzoli today, offers an intimate look at the homes and studios of some of Europe’s best known designers, including Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto, Carlo Mollino, Gae Aulenti and Finn Juhl, alongside lesser known names like Roland Rainer, Joseph Nemec and Renaat Braem. It follows Williamson’s first book, “Handcrafted Modern: At Home With Midcentury Designers” (Rizzoli, 2010). Both titles are part of a larger project Williamson began almost 10 years ago. “I made a dream list of the homes of all the architects and designers I wanted to visit in my lifetime,” she explains. “I’ve always been a fan of design, and I was curious to see how these people — whose work I love and am inspired by — lived themselves.”

docs.lead_paragraph: On a recent evening, over a couple of half-pints of lager (served rather icy, by British standards, at £1.50, or $2.45, each), the writer Ruth Cherrington reclined in the maroon upholstered lounge of the Langham Working Men’s Club in North London. The scene was quiet. The barmaid hovered near the bar’s sole patron: a white-haired gentleman in a leather coat who was watching the BBC’s “Great British Bake Off” on TV. Mr. Hannigan, 49, who has been director general of defense and intelligence at the Foreign Office since 2010, will take over from Iain Lobban when he steps down in the fall, Foreign Secretary William Hague announced. Officials have denied that Mr. Lobban’s departure is linked to the controversy over the close relationship between GCHQ and the N.S.A., which was revealed in documents leaked by the former American intelligence contractor Edward J. Snowden. Under pressure to be more transparent, Mr. Lobban became the first head of the agency last November to give evidence in public before lawmakers.

docs.lead_paragraph: Judges on Tuesday refused to throw out two charges of genocide against the former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, saying there is enough evidence for his war-crimes trial to continue on all counts. Under tribunal rules, charges can be dropped if evidence is seen as insufficient after the prosecution rests its case, which it did this year. Over the course of 200 hours, prosecutors brought 164 live witnesses and used thousands of documents — including Mr. Mladic’s own war logs — to make their case. Among other charges, Mr. Mladic, 72, is accused of waging a campaign of ethnic cleansing to drive non-Serbs from ethnically mixed regions of the former Yugoslavia, and of involvement in the mass killing of more than 7,000 unarmed men in Srebrenica.

headline.main: The Hague: Charges Stand for Mladic

docs.lead_paragraph: Get your popcorn ready. The Tribeca Film Festival, now in its 13th year, returns to downtown Manhattan today to host 12 days of obsessive moviegoing and compelling conversation about film. Co-founded in 2002 by the actor Robert De Niro with his producing partner Jane Rosenthal and the real estate financier Craig Hatkoff, the festival was originally conceived as a cultural response to Sept. 11. And while its reach has expanded significantly over the years — a staggering 6,117 films were submitted for this year’s festival, increasing both the quality and diversity of the offerings (fans will remember, though they might prefer not to, that “Star Wars Episode II: The Clone Wars” premiered at the inaugural fest) — the spirit of the original outing has remained intact.

docs.lead_paragraph: Carla Fernández is an artist and activist whose medium is fashion. She works with traditional textiles from her native Mexico to create contemporary designs, supporting and nurturing artisan communities in the process. Now her work gets the museum treatment in a new show, “The Barefoot Designer: A Passion for Radical Design and Community,” the first-ever fashion exhibit at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. Through fashion photographs and drawings, garments, video and performance, the show explores the techniques of master artisans from each of Mexico’s five states, and Fernández’s method for designing with them using the rectangular and square patterns of indigenous garments, a technique she calls “the square root.” By incorporating these ancient methods into a modern fashion line, “we are fast-forwarding tradition,” she says.

headline.main: On View | Turning Ancient Craft Techniques Into Modern Fashion

docs.abstract: The law’s supporters should define what kind of specific outcomes they expect.
docs.snippet: The law’s supporters should define what kind of specific outcomes they expect.
docs.lead_paragraph: Ezra Klein, in his new capacity as one of the impresarios behind Vox, has written a pair of attention-grabbing posts — here, and then here — defending the proposition that Obamacare has, in some sense, “won,” and that conservatives who can’t come to terms with that victory can’t come to terms with reality itself. Reading them, it struck me that this argument would benefit from laying down some specific markers for the near future, because Klein seems to move back and forth between two definitions of success. At times, as when he writes that Obamacare “has won its survival” and allows that that “there are still many good critiques to make” of the law, he seems to be using a narrow definition, with which I mostly agree — the law won’t collapse under its own weight, the enrollment levels are high enough to make a return to the coverage status quo ante unlikely, etc. But when he uses language like “the individual mandate … is working” and “the law is back on its expected track,” and concludes that “[Kathleen Sebelius] can leave with the law she helped build looking, shockingly, like a success,” it implies a stronger definition of victory, in which Obamacare isn’t just continuing, isn’t just unlikely to be swiftly repealed, but is clearly succeeding as a policy in basically the way its advocates predicted that it would.

headline.main: For Obamacare, What Counts As Success?

docs.snippet: In a new book, “The Inspired Home: Nests of Creatives,” two creative types with a good eye for design share images of 17 homes, handpicked for their owners’ personal style.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the new book “The Inspired Home: Nests of Creatives” (Rizzoli, $55), Kim Ficaro and Todd Nickey prove that the most inspiring homes are not always the ones dreamed up by architects, designers or the incredibly wealthy. And they should know: Ficaro has styled props and interiors for Bon Appétit, Town & Country, Elle, Harper’s Bazaar and Domino, while Nickey co-owns a successful design company in L.A. Rather than choosing homes simply because they struck their fancy, the co-authors first rounded up a trove of creative types — artists, writers, musicians, stylists, art directors — who had interesting personal style, and then hoped their homes would follow suit. Their instincts proved correct, and the 17 nests featured in this beautiful coffee-table book, shot by the Danish photographer Ditte Isager, reveal the inspiring combination of natural light and accidental, lived-in beauty. And despite the authors’ professions, Ficaro and Nickey opted not to style or decorate any of the interiors before they were photographed. “We wanted to let the places breathe on their own,” explains Ficaro.

headline.main: Bookshelf | Homes Inspired by the Creative Lives of their Owners

docs.lead_paragraph: On the afternoon before my college graduation in 1999, there was a ceremony for graduates who were getting department prizes. My father was a New York City tunnel worker (a “sandhog”) and at that time he was working on Roosevelt Island, a 20-minute drive from Barnard’s campus. He always showered before leaving the job site, and on that day he’d brought khakis, a freshly pressed shirt and tie and the new jacket my mother had gotten him for his 55th birthday. I remember what he was wearing because it was the first time I noticed him holding a handkerchief, which he used throughout the ceremony to dab the corners of his mouth. After, when we were discussing where to have dinner, I spotted a narrow river of saliva traveling down the side of his chin.

headline.main: My Father’s Strength

docs.lead_paragraph: The United Nations refugee agency said Wednesday that it was working with 14 other humanitarian relief groups to seek $274 million in emergency donations to support the swelling population of refugees fleeing violence in the Central African Republic, one of Africa’s most dysfunctional countries. The refugee agency said nearly 200,000 residents had escaped to neighboring countries over the last four months. More than 600,000 people were displaced inside the Central African Republic because of communal violence that has effectively partitioned the country into Christian and Muslim sectors. António Guterres, the United Nations high commissioner for refugees, said in a statement that all relief agencies working in the region were “dramatically underfunded” and that his own agency was far outspending what it had expected. “This cannot be sustained,” he said.

headline.main: Central African Republic: Aid Sought for Those Fleeing Unrest

docs.snippet: The clever designer, whose fans include Kanye West and Sienna Miller, just debuted a new range at Bergdorf Goodman and Dover Street Market New York.
docs.lead_paragraph: “Fine jewelry,” says the designer and sculptor Bibi van der Velden, “should be taken with a dose of humor.” A thread of whimsy runs through the work of the New York-born, Amsterdam-based designer, whose handcrafted pieces have been collected by the likes of Kanye West and Sienna Miller. Though she started her line in 2006, her work is gaining new attention this season; it recently debuted at Bergdorf Goodman and Dover Street Market in New York and will launch on Net-a-Porter on June 9th. Her spring collection, carved from 40,000-year-old mammoth tusks that emerged from the Russian tundra thanks to global warming, includes such designs as a pendant depicting a cloud raining thunderbolts, a necklace strung with dodo egg-shaped “pearls” and a wraparound dragon ring that features a tiny man clutching a diamond emerging from the jaws of the beast. The natural world is a leitmotif for van der Velden, who likes to tell the story of how an owl once soared through the room at one of her runway shows. For fall, her pieces will incorporate actual scarab wings. “I am fascinated by nature and its beauty,” she says. “I hate to see such beauty go to waste.”

headline.main: Bibi van der Velden’s Whimsical Fine Jewelry Collection

docs.snippet: Notes on a frontrunner-less Republican field.
docs.lead_paragraph: Right now, the most striking thing about the public polling on the 2016 Republican nomination isn’t just the absence of a clear frontrunner: It’s the absence of a clear pair or trio or even a quartet of frontrunners. The latest Iowa poll has Mike Huckabee in the pole position with eleven percent, and then eight (!) others — all of whom are more serious figures than some of the characters who briefly polled well last time around — bunched between six and ten percent; the national polling average isn’t quite that compressed, but it’s close. This can’t last, but everyone recognizes that the situation is historically unusual (as, on the other side, is Hillary Clinton’s extraordinary advantage); the question is, how unusual, and what does it mean for the normal way that these things shake out?

headline.main: The Party Decides, Unless It Can’t

docs.abstract: Many locals still haven’t heard of all the next big things: flashy new art galleries, dynamically developing old neighborhoods, great bars — beyond and including beer — and new restaurants.
docs.snippet: Many locals still haven’t heard of all the next big things: flashy new art galleries, dynamically developing old neighborhoods, great bars — beyond and including beer — and new restaurants.
docs.lead_paragraph: For people who haven’t traveled to Prague recently, the Czech capital might seem like a known quantity: a city with a thousand years of architecture, cheap beer and often boring restaurants where the most unusual ingredients are the doughy dumplings. But Prague is developing so quickly that many locals still haven’t heard of all the next big things: flashy new art galleries, dynamically developing old neighborhoods, great bars — beyond and including beer — and new restaurants with flavorful offerings from classic steaks and chops to Asian spice. In fact, so many new developments have appeared in Prague that you could spend an entire weekend visiting only those places that have opened in the past couple of years. See Prague Castle, Charles Bridge and all the other classic attractions. But finish out your stay with some of the vibrant newcomers.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Prague

docs.abstract: If you’re the type of traveler who likes to go beyond guides to develop a sense of place, one of these recently published or about-to-be-published books could be for you.
docs.snippet: If you’re the type of traveler who likes to go beyond guides to develop a sense of place, one of these recently published or about-to-be-published books could be for you.
docs.lead_paragraph: Paris, London, Venice: hardly the most mysterious places on the planet. Yet beyond Notre Dame, Big Ben and the Basilica di San Marco lie hidden iterations of these well-trodden cities: obscure corners, faded histories and the daily pleasures and aggravations of those who live there. A 19th-century Parisian photographer, a former musician in London and a novelist in Venice are among those who offer unexpected insights in six recently published or about-to-be-published books. Some urge you to visit, others beg you to stay away, all are likely to trigger the wanderlust of those eager to get closer to the authentic heart of a place.

headline.main: Portraits on the Page of Paris, London and Venice
headline.print_headline: The City Within

docs.lead_paragraph: It’s a daring thing to write about an evil person, especially in this day of autobiographical fiction, when readers assume most characters are thinly veiled self-portraits. And yet evil characters are usually dynamic and fascinating, upstaging all the goody-goodies. Think of Milton’s blazing, sexy Satan; Balzac’s scheming, driven master criminal, Vautrin; or Shakespeare’s Iago. Despite the allure of such characters, writers today usually avoid them, maybe because the whole category of Evil seems too theological or because modern psychology assumes that every bad act can be traced to childhood neglect or abuse and thus be explained away. I have to give my students an assignment to write about bad guys in order to get them to do it. But when they do write about them, it’s such a release!

docs.abstract: Adam Begley’s biography of John Updike surveys his work as well as his life.
docs.snippet: Adam Begley’s biography of John Updike surveys his work as well as his life.
docs.lead_paragraph: At first, he wanted to be a graphic artist. In 1954, John Updike — age 22, newly married and fresh out of Harvard, where he’d studied English literature and taken art courses — was awarded a fellowship to study abroad, and decided to apply to the Ruskin School of Drawing and Fine Arts in Oxford, England. Asked to explain this decision, Updike replied, “It’s always been my ambition to be the next Walt Disney.” During his childhood in Shillington, Pa., where he lived until the age of 13 and which his readers know through his Olinger stories, his mother, Linda, arranged for her prodigiously talented son to take lessons from a local artist. Later, when they moved to Plowville, 11 miles from Shillington, to a farmhouse he would describe in his novel “Of the Farm,” Updike — now 14 or 15 — began sending his drawings and cartoons to The New Yorker and other publications. For Updike, who was interested in drawing but also, like his mother, in writing, to be published in The New Yorker had been an ambition, if not an obsession, from the moment the magazine first entered the household when he was 12.

headline.main: Updike at Rest

docs.lead_paragraph: I fell in love with a girl in high school. Nothing happened romantically between us, but we did hang out a few times. Eight years later, walking through a grocery store with my partner, I saw her again. She didn’t acknowledge me; she may not have seen me. But I felt a torrent of emotions. We are different people now, and I am with someone I care for deeply. But something about seeing her unsettled me. Whatever I felt for her, I’ve never felt again. And several times a year, I imagine my life with her in it. What should I do?

docs.abstract: “Transcendence” stars Johnny Depp as an artificial-intelligence genius whose wife uploads his consciousness into a supermachine after anti-technology extremists shoot him.
docs.snippet: “Transcendence” stars Johnny Depp as an artificial-intelligence genius whose wife uploads his consciousness into a supermachine after anti-technology extremists shoot him.
docs.lead_paragraph: Johnny Depp, who’s built a brilliant career despite many of his lamentable film choices, may not be the first actor you think of to play a genius — much less humanity’s destroyer or savior. But he’s weirdly perfect in “Transcendence,” an inelegant, no doubt implausible (maybe not) science-fiction film about a futurist whose consciousness is uploaded onto the Internet. There, he (or a mysterious vestige of his being) expands like the universe, growing larger and mutating into a being who is godlike and yet far from divine, sort of like a star at the apex of his popularity.

docs.lead_paragraph: The title character in “Fading Gigolo,” a low-key, low-energy comedy about New York haves and have-nots, is Fioravante, a melancholic bookstore employee played by the film’s director, John Turturro. When you first meet Fioravante, he’s packing up boxes, on the verge of becoming an ex-bookstore employee. His boss, Murray (Woody Allen), has been forced to shutter his charming shop, a painful and all-too-frequent occurrence in the real New York. docs.abstract: The faces in “Manakamana,” by Stephanie Spray and Pacho Velez, stare into the camera, out into space and, perhaps, into the great beyond.
docs.snippet: The faces in “Manakamana,” by Stephanie Spray and Pacho Velez, stare into the camera, out into space and, perhaps, into the great beyond.
docs.lead_paragraph: The faces in “Manakamana,” a transporting ethnographic film set in a green sliver of Nepal, stare into the camera, out into space and, perhaps, into the great beyond. The faces are sometimes creased and weathered, sometimes smooth as pebbles. A few look etched with worry, as if they were weighed down by a heavy burden, although they may also be seized with fear. That’s because for 10 or so minutes at a time, these faces are floating hundreds of feet above a lush Nepali forest in a cable car that takes pilgrims to and from the temple that gives this film its rhythmic title.

headline.main: Soaring Trips to a Temple in Nepal

docs.lead_paragraph: Turkey’s Parliament on Thursday passed a bill that increases the powers of the national spy agency and strengthens its immunity, a move that critics said would allow Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan to bolster his control over state institutions. The measure, which requires presidential approval before it becomes a law, would give the National Intelligence Organization, known by the initials of its Turkish name M.I.T., access to information collected by public and private institutions without a court order and would expand its ability to carry out covert operations. Government officials said the changes would make the agency more efficient and provide protections for its personnel. Mr. Erdogan has been tightening his grip on state agencies as his government deals with accusations of corruption and has tried to block or control access to the Internet, Twitter and YouTube. “With this legislation, the M.I.T. is no longer a national intelligence agency but has become the prime minister’s intelligence agency,” said an opposition lawmaker, Sezgin Tanrikulu.

He was taken to a hospital in Goma, where he underwent surgery. Mr. de Merode, above, is a Belgian prince and is married to Louise Leakey, a Kenyan paleontologist and the granddaughter of the archaeologist Louis Leakey, known for his studies on human evolution in Africa. Virunga National Park was established in 1925 by Belgium, which then governed Congo.

docs.lead_paragraph: Then and now, the rugged on-screen apparel of the cinematic heroes Clint Eastwood and John Wayne serves as an iconic expression of American style. This season, their characters’ Wild West legacy lives on in fashion’s frontier as the influence for spring collections by the likes of Junya Watanabe, Paco Rabanne, Creatures of the Wind and Valentino. Designers took visual cues from the cowboy uniform — distressed denim, fringe, turquoise, embroidery and, of course, boots — to create separates that come together for a fully transportive look. But if a head-to-toe Annie Oakley-influenced ensemble isn’t your modus operandi, pairing any of these individual items with monochromatic basics — a white tee with Junya Watanabe jeans or a black dress with a cashmere Elder Statesman bandana — will keep things relevant and fresh.

docs.lead_paragraph: 9 P.M. (Nat Geo Wild) CESAR MILLAN: LOVE MY PIT BULL Once upon a time, the pit bull was a popular family pet beloved by President Theodore Roosevelt, Gen. George S. Patton and Helen Keller. Today, these dogs are more closely associated with gangs and dogfighting, and have been responsible for a large percentage of fatal dog attacks on humans. Pit bulls are often abused or abandoned, and are euthanized at a higher rate than other dogs, with an estimated one million put down each year in the United States. In this special, Mr. Millan chronicles the history of the pit bull as a herder and companion — in Britain, the Staffordshire bull terrier was nicknamed “the nanny dog” for its sweet disposition with children — and with his own pit bull, Junior (above, with Mr. Millan), makes the case for the dogs as loyal and loving, given the right training for both animals and humans. “All dogs are great companions,” he says. “Communication creates a partnership, and dogs have the simplest communication on the planet. For them, everything is about trust, respect and love.”

docs.abstract: In a video for her song “Cherry on Top,” which premieres here, the Swedish chanteuse comes to terms with the loss of her previous career as a dancer.
docs.snippet: In a video for her song “Cherry on Top,” which premieres here, the Swedish chanteuse comes to terms with the loss of her previous career as a dancer.
docs.lead_paragraph: Before she came to public attention as the ethereal electro-pop siren Oh Land, the Danish musician Nanna Fabricius was a small-town girl who dreamed of becoming a ballerina. She left home for Stockholm at age 15 to pursue those ambitions until a back injury ended her career. Still, she often dreams about her first creative pursuit. An actual dream, in fact, inspired her new music video for “Cherry on Top,” a twinkling ballad on her 2013 album “Wish Bone,” produced by TV on the Radio’s Dave Sitek. In it, she went into a dance studio — only to discover that she wasn’t a dancer, she was a piano player. docs.lead_paragraph: Hindsight is a wonderful thing. But in fiction it can take on a whole new power — blunderingly obvious or brightly illuminating, depending on how imaginatively it’s applied. Rare is the contemporary novel that doesn’t set out, at least in part, to examine the effects of past behavior on present outcomes. While this can lead to pungent and suspenseful storytelling, it requires a delicate balance, keeping the reader engaged in the narrative momentum of an unknown future that’s already in the past. In her perceptive, empathetic and often emotionally gripping new novel, Leah Hager Cohen — author of the acclaimed “The Grief of Others” — has managed the trick very deftly.

This coincidence — only the first of many in Ackroyd’s breezy contrivance of a novel — signals an “invisible communion” among the brothers that will link their fates even as they set out on radically different paths through life. In the end, true to the Grimm Brothers template, only one will endure his personal ordeal and emerge relatively unscathed; the other two wind up succumbing to the wiles of the true hero of the piece — the city of London itself, the only character in the book the author actually seems to care about.

docs.lead_paragraph: Plato has begun to appear in some unexpected places. On the first track of Jay-Z and Kanye West’s hip-hop album, “Watch the Throne” (2011), you can pick out the line, “Is Pious pious cause God loves pious?” This, as classicists will instantly recognize, is an allusion to a dilemma posed in Plato’s dialogue “Euthyphro,” in which Socrates asks, “Is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or is it pious because it is loved by the gods?” In Rebecca Newberger Goldstein’s new book, “Plato at the Googleplex: Why Philosophy Won’t Go Away,” Plato turns up not only at the search engine’s headquarters in Mountain View, Calif., but also with the obstreperous host of a cable news talk show, as a consultant to an advice columnist, and in several other places a long way from ancient Athens. In Goldstein’s neat finale, the pupil of Socrates and teacher of Aristotle eagerly disappears into the magnetic bowels of an fM.R.I. scanner to have his brain probed.

docs.lead_paragraph: In the summer of 1981, a Swedish graduate student named Svante Paabo filled a laboratory at the University of Uppsala with the stench of rotting liver. Paabo was supposed to be studying viruses, but he had become secretly obsessed with a more exotic line of research: extracting DNA from Egyptian mummies. No one at the time had any idea if the desiccated flesh of pharaohs still contained any genetic material, so Paabo decided to run an experiment. He bought a piece of calf’s liver and put it in a lab oven at about 120 degrees for a few days to approximate mummification. In the dried, blackened lump of meat, he succeeded in finding scattered fragments of DNA.

It has been uninhabited for 50 years and off limits to all but biologists for more than a decade; the city manages it as a nature preserve. docs.abstract: In hindsight, the 1964 New York World’s Fair, thought at the time to be a celebration of modernity, seems instead like the tail end of something, the petering out of what was essentially a 19th-century phenomenon.
docs.snippet: In hindsight, the 1964 New York World’s Fair, thought at the time to be a celebration of modernity, seems instead like the tail end of something, the petering out of what was essentially a 19th-century phenomenon.
docs.lead_paragraph: When you drive by on the Van Wyck Expressway or the Grand Central Parkway, the space-age towers of the New York State Pavilion, among the few remaining traces of the 1964 New York World’s Fair, rise up from the trees like a relic of some vanished, Jetsonian civilization, and the people who built them seem much more than 50 years distant from us. They were people apparently inspired by the idea of progress, and by a now quaint-seeming faith in the future, who actually believed in things like world’s fairs. Who would think of organizing such an event now? Who would pay for it? Who would bother to go?

headline.main: The Fair to End All Fairs

docs.abstract: After the 1964 New York World’s Fair closed on Oct. 17, 1965, the fair was carefully and willfully dismantled.
docs.snippet: After the 1964 New York World’s Fair closed on Oct. 17, 1965, the fair was carefully and willfully dismantled.
docs.lead_paragraph: One day, the New York World’s Fair, with its architecture flavored by the Space Age, was the future. Then the next day, it was history. After the debt-plagued fair closed on Oct. 17, 1965, the destruction began. Over the course of a year, as these striking images from 1965 and ’66 attest, the fair was carefully and willfully dismantled: Cranes were brought in to remove the exhibitions, buildings were demolished, and even before the official closing, people picked over the grounds, yanking plants from their beds as souvenirs.

But few visitors are aware that the child is the son of the Count Altamira, governor of what was the Banco de San Carlos (now the Banco de España) and that between 1786 and 1788 the count commissioned Goya to paint that portrait, along with three others.

docs.abstract: “A Royal Passion: Queen Victoria and Photography,” at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, reveals a monarch who quickly adopted a new art form and used it for her own purposes.
docs.snippet: “A Royal Passion: Queen Victoria and Photography,” at the Getty Museum in Los Angeles, reveals a monarch who quickly adopted a new art form and used it for her own purposes.
docs.lead_paragraph: LOS ANGELES — Today, as the formal boundaries between the British royal family and the public narrow, pictures of 9-month-old Prince George are posted daily on the Facebook pages of Prince William and the Duchess of Cambridge, the former Kate Middleton. But, in fact, photography has been promoting the royal brand since its inception in the 19th century, as an exhibition on view at the Getty Center here shows. Fame may seem a 20th-century phenomenon, but Queen Victoria was the first public figure to exploit its promotional potential and the earliest — and least likely — international celebrity of the photographed world.

headline.main: Love Those Royal Family Photos? It All Started With Victoria.

docs.lead_paragraph: Ukraine has asked the International Criminal Court to investigate the deaths of civilians on its territory that occurred from Nov. 21, 2013, to Feb. 22, covering the period when more than 100 people were killed during antigovernment protests. It excludes the period shortly afterward when Russia annexed Crimea. It was not immediately clear whom Ukraine was accusing of the deaths. Initially, Parliament sought to single out the former president, Viktor F. Yanukovych, but other groups may also be included. Because Ukraine is not a member of the court, it has formally given it jurisdiction with respect to the period in question. That step, which was apparently taken in early April, was announced in a court statement issued late Thursday. Ukraine’s application said it expected “that the court shall duly study the case.” But a court spokesman emphasized that it would be up to a prosecutor to decide whether to proceed, and then the court’s judges would be asked to approve the decision. An investigation is not expected any time soon.

headline.main: Ukraine Seeks Inquiry Into Killings

docs.snippet: The viral disease known as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome has reached Asia, according to reports from Malaysia and the Philippines.
docs.lead_paragraph: The viral disease known as Middle East Respiratory Syndrome has reached Asia, according to reports from Malaysia and the Philippines. The Malaysian Health Ministry said a 54-year-old man recently back from a pilgrimage to Mecca, Saudi Arabia, died of it on Sunday, and a Filipino nurse was quarantined, along with his family, after a positive blood test. The nurse appeared healthy but, before returning to Manila on Tuesday, had been in contact with a Filipino paramedic in the United Arab Emirates who died of MERS. On Wednesday, the Emirates reported 10 new cases, all among health workers who treated a MERS patient who died April 10. Since the disease was discovered in 2012, there have been 243 confirmed cases with 93 deaths, the World Health Organization said. The coronavirus that causes MERS appears to originate in bats and is widespread in Middle Eastern camel herds. It occasionally infects humans and can spread among them, usually only after close contact.

headline.main: Viral Disease Spreads to Southeast Asia

Opposition leaders who boycotted the election immediately cast doubt on the results, accusing Mr. Bouteflika, left, and his supporters of widespread fraud and of inflating the turnout, which was officially 51.7 percent. His strongest challenger, former Prime Minister Ali Benflis, won only 12 percent of the vote. Mr. Bouteflika, 77, has been largely incapacitated since suffering a stroke last year, but he has managed to retain a strong grip on power and has avoided the democratic changes prompted by the Arab Spring uprisings elsewhere in North Africa. He cast his ballot in the presidential election on Thursday from a wheelchair.

docs.lead_paragraph: THE bedroom was no wider than a subway car, painted Q-train yellow, and had a window facing a construction site that jackhammered at all hours. But I couldn’t wait to move in. I’d answered a Craigslist ad to join a new communal home, and though I wasn’t sure I was the communal-home type, I was also in a phase of reconsidering what type of person I might be. My six housemates planned to open a collectively owned and operated bed-and-breakfast in our building. If our projected costs and occupancy rates were correct (and if the jackhammering would let up), each partner would work 10 to 15 hours a week at the co-op to cover our rent, utilities and shared groceries, freeing up time to pursue the low-to-zero-pay projects we all had in music, art, education and writing.

docs.abstract: A bit more of the Kristof family background in Ukraine, and reader comments on my column from my father’s native village
docs.snippet: A bit more of the Kristof family background in Ukraine, and reader comments on my column from my father’s native village
docs.lead_paragraph: For my Sunday column, I returned to the village near Chernivtsi, Ukraine, where my father grew up. What struck me there was the deep yearning for connections to the West, for a future tied not with Russia but with Western Europe. Obviously, one encounters somewhat different sentiments in eastern Ukraine, but overall this popular yearning for a future in Europe runs both deep and broad.

docs.lead_paragraph: Elsie de Wolfe favored flowery painting on walls and furniture, mirrored surfaces to reflect light and an overall brightness for the rooms she designed. docs.abstract: During the Holy Week in Paris in 1914, streams of Parisians left the city for the Easter vacation, while tourists arrived to explore the capital.
docs.snippet: During the Holy Week in Paris in 1914, streams of Parisians left the city for the Easter vacation, while tourists arrived to explore the capital.
docs.lead_paragraph: Two distinct streams of people could have been noticed outside the various Paris railway termini yesterday, the first consisting of Parisians about to quit the city for the Easter vacation, and the second, composed of English, German and other tourists, who had just arrived bent upon passing the same gay period in exploring the French capital. The result of the ingress of tourists was that the boulevards and main streets of Paris presented an even more cosmopolitan appearance than usual. Fortunately fine weather favored the sightseers and the guides reaped a rich silver harvest. Groups of energetic Teutons made an almost military inspection of the Louvre and decided with unanimity that the Mona Lisa’s smile is as over-rated as it is ambiguous.The char-à-bancs were all crowded, the majority of the passengers wearing caps. At dusk a group of English tourists, who had probably crossed the Channel for the sake of higher mental culture, marched contentedly up the avenue de l’Opéra to the immortal strains of “You made me love you,” supplied by the youngest visitor’s richly toned mouth-organ. The Frenchmen who had remained in Paris gazed upon their progress with unspeakable admiration and drank a thoughtful aperitif to the eternal durability of the “Entente Cordiale.” — The New York Herald, European edition, April 12, 1914.

headline.main: 1914: Easter Scenes In Paris

docs.lead_paragraph: 3 P.M. (FX Movie Channel) HEREAFTER (2010) Clint Eastwood imagines what happens after people die by braiding together three story lines, each involving a collision between the living and the dead. In San Francisco, George Lonegan (Matt Damon, above), who receives messages from the deceased loved ones of anyone he touches, chooses a life of obscurity instead of exploiting his gift. In London, a solemn boy named Marcus feels the presence of his twin, Jason, whose violent death has left him adrift. (The brothers are played by George and Frankie McLaren.) And in Paris, Marie Lelay (Cécile de France), who nearly died in the 2004 tsunami in South Asia, is convinced that she has seen a metaphysical reality the world is determined to ignore. “Persuasion is not really the point, though if anyone could make me believe in ghosts, it would be Clint Eastwood,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times of this film, written by Peter Morgan. He added: “What does seem new — newly strange, newly beautiful — is what ‘Hereafter’ makes of the here and now. It is a curious movie in both senses of the word: an unusual experience and an open-ended inquiry into something nobody can really claim to understand. It leaves you wondering, which may be the most fitting way of saying that it’s wonderful.”

But lately I’ve been buying thick stalks of asparagus, and all I want to do is roast it; roasting intensifies the flavor and the stalks become incredibly succulent, more so than when the asparagus is steamed. This quality isn’t lost even when the sliced stalks are hidden inside a quiche.

docs.lead_paragraph: Spring onions found their way into several of this week’s quiches. For this one, I cooked the onions with cabbage – even a half a head of cabbage that has been lingering in your refrigerator will work here – until both vegetables were soft, lightly colored and sweet. I added caraway seeds to the mix because I love the flavor of caraway with cabbage. I used 1/2 teaspoon, just enough so that people noticed; they couldn’t recognize what it was (“Cumin?” they asked) right away, but they liked it. I made the filling a day ahead and let it sit uncovered overnight in the refrigerator.

I figured if it worked so well in that dish, it could also in a quiche. It does.

docs.abstract: This dough, made with half whole-wheat flour, has a nutty, rich flavor that works well for a savory tart.
docs.snippet: This dough, made with half whole-wheat flour, has a nutty, rich flavor that works well for a savory tart.
docs.lead_paragraph: Most of the vegetable tarts that I post on Recipes for Health call for a yeasted olive oil crust that I love to work with. With French quiches, however, I prefer a crust that resembles classic French pastry. However, I always use at least half whole-wheat flour – which is not so French – not only for its nutritional superiority, but also because it gives the resulting shell a nuttier, richer flavor that is particularly welcome in a savory tart. This dough, adapted from Jacquy Pfeiffer’s recipe for pâte brisée in “The Art of French Pastry,” involves more butter than you’re used to seeing in my recipes, but an occasional butter-based crust, especially when it’s made with whole-wheat flour and contains a filling that is all about vegetables, is not going to kill us. Instead, it’s a vehicle for the foods that we want to move toward the center of our plates.

headline.main: Whole-Wheat Pie Dough

It’s not so much that what Sargent said is wrong, although some of his principles are by no means universally agreed upon, even in normal times. docs.lead_paragraph: Our puzzle this week is about a tricky kind of relationship — one that’s a bit counterintuitive. Normally, when we compare several things, we expect something like the following: your friend Agnes weighs more than Beatrice, and Beatrice weighs more than Clarissa, then we’d expect Agnes to outweigh Clarissa. This makes sense. This kind of relationship would also work for heights, ages, and other single-dimension measures. This also works for containers: a dime is in a small pouch in Clarissa’s purse, so the dime is in the purse.

Somewhere a dictatorial “patriarch” is still having his rival cooked and served up to his dinner guests on a great dish; an old colonel is waiting for a letter that never comes; a beautiful young girl is being prostituted by her heartless grandmother; and a kindlier patriarch, José Arcadio Buendía, one of the founders of the new settlement of Macondo, a man interested in science and alchemy, is declaring to his horrified wife that “the earth is round, like an orange.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Two Unicef staff members who were abducted last week in Pakistan’s southern port city of Karachi have been released, a spokesman for the United Nations secretary general, Ban Ki-moon, said Monday. The spokesman, Stéphane Dujarric, said the two were safe and well, but he had no other details. It was not clear who had abducted them or why they had been freed. Foreign aid workers in Pakistan have been increasingly singled out by jihadist insurgents for kidnappings and attacks. At least 12 United Nations staff members have been killed in Pakistan since January 2009. Some of the assaults have been tied to Taliban retributions for efforts by Unicef and other international aid groups to vaccinate children against polio, which has been spreading in Pakistan, particularly in the northwest tribal areas. Some Taliban leaders have said vaccine workers are Western spies using the guise of humanitarian aid to gather intelligence information.

docs.lead_paragraph: A Justice Department official denied Monday that the F.B.I. had investigated how a manifesto by Khalid Shaikh Mohammed ended up at The Huffington Post. It came to light last week that agents had approached a member of the defense team for a detainee facing trial before a military commission over the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. He was asked to sign a confidentiality agreement, something the defense lawyers said improperly made him an informant. The disclosure derailed a week of pretrial hearings, and the special trial counsel, Fernando Campoamor-Sanchez, an assistant United States attorney, is leading an investigation into the matter. It was widely speculated that the subject of the F.B.I. inquiry was how the 36-page manuscript by Mr. Mohammed — the self-described architect of the attacks — had been leaked. But in a public court filing on Monday, Mr. Campoamor-Sanchez said that was not true. He did not identify the investigation’s actual subject, although he apparently offered greater details to the judge in an accompanying classified filing.

headline.main: Official Denies F.B.I. Was Investigating Manifesto Leak

docs.lead_paragraph: 9 P.M. (13, 49) A FIERCE GREEN FIRE (2013) At one time, it was about the dams. The naturalist John Muir and the forester Gifford Pinchot waged war in the early 1900s over the flooding of the magnificent Hetch Hetchy Valley in Yosemite National Park. Decades later, the proposed damming of the Colorado River prompted public outrage, and the environmental movement was born. Today some two million organizations worldwide work on behalf of social justice and the environment. In this Earth Day tribute, “American Masters” chronicles issues (pollution, whaling, conservation of the Amazon rain forest, climate change) within the fight and the players who made a difference (Lois Gibbs, who rallied on behalf of Love Canal; David Brower, above, the first executive director of the Sierra Club; and Paul Watson and Rex Weyler, the founders of Greenpeace). “The environmental movement is about nature versus humanity,” says Robert Redford, who with Meryl Streep, Ashley Judd, Van Jones and Isabel Allende narrates this documentary, directed by Mark Kitchell. “It arose at a time when our industrial civilization has grown so powerful it threatens the natural world on which we depend for survival. It has become the battle for a living planet.”

docs.abstract: A quick look shows what has happened to incomes in recent decades.
docs.snippet: A quick look shows what has happened to incomes in recent decades.
docs.lead_paragraph: In 1980, the American rich and middle class and most of the poor had higher incomes than their counterparts almost anywhere in the world. But incomes for the middle class and poor in the United States have since been growing more slowly than elsewhere. Why? Among the reasons: This country has lost its once-wide lead in educational attainment. Other countries have increased their workers’ skill levels more quickly, helping create well-paying jobs. The United States also tolerates more inequality: The minimum wage is lower here. Executives make more money. The government redistributes less of it. By 2010, the poor in several other countries had pulled ahead. And Canada’s median income had reached a virtual tie with that of the United States. Since 2010, other data suggest Canada has moved ahead.

headline.main: This simple table summarizes our story on American living standards.

docs.lead_paragraph: After graduating from New York University in 2013 with a degree in film and television, Dan Kim found himself in an entirely unexpected situation: a friend asked him to help shoot a music video, an incredible opportunity at the time, and Kim had to turn him down. “I was in film school, but I didn’t know anybody who could help,” he explains, referencing his then-nonexistent set of industry contacts. “I thought it was insane that there was no space for people like me to share their ideas. People still use Craigslist!” The realization drove Kim to create Unique Board, a website where artists working in seven different categories – cinematography, fashion, design, music, art, dance/performance and technology/programming – can find each other for different projects. “We’re digitizing the collaboration process, making it simple but effective by cutting off all the extra steps of networking,” Kim explains about the site, which has amassed over 200 members — many based in New York, many others international — since going live in February.

headline.main: An Online Meeting Place for Creative Types

docs.lead_paragraph: Craig Zadan and Neil Meron, whose production of this year’s largely successful Academy Awards eclipsed their Seth MacFarlane-led show of 2013, will return to produce the Oscar show for the third consecutive year. Where the 2013 show might be best remembered for Mr. MacFarlane’s flat-footed musical ode to actresses’ bare breasts, the 2014 show’s most-enduring image was of the star-filled selfie, above, snapped by a sunny Ellen DeGeneres. This year’s show also drew 45.4 million viewers, according to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, the most in 10 years. Dawn Hudson, the Academy’s chief executive, said in a statement that Mr. Zadan and Mr. Meron were “masters at tapping into the zeitgeist and capturing the hearts of movie fans around the world.” Mr. Zadan and Mr. Meron have a long history of bringing Broadway musicals to the big and little screens: They produced the film versions of “Chicago” and “Hairspray,” are in the process of producing “Pippin,” and for television have made “Annie,” “Rogers & Hammerstein’s Cinderella” and “Gypsy.” The 87th Academy Awards will be next Feb. 22, at the Dolby Theater in Hollywood. No host has been named.

docs.abstract: The slipping economic advantages of the American middle class.
docs.snippet: The slipping economic advantages of the American middle class.
docs.lead_paragraph: Last week, in a tax day post defending the virtues of light taxation, I discussed the various economic advantages that the United States of America has reaped from its lower-than-average tax burden, and the evidence that not only the U.S. but also our developed-world peers have benefited from the American style of free market capitalism. But I concluded by allowing that this argument would look that much weaker the longer the U.S. economy goes without delivering on the second half of the basic American “more risk and more inequality for more growth and jobs and self-sufficiency” bargain — a combination which has held historically, but not so much of late.

docs.abstract: I didn’t want to be pregnant, and at the time, I couldn’t enjoy it on any level. Now, watching friends anticipate birth, I want what I know what I missed.
docs.snippet: I didn’t want to be pregnant, and at the time, I couldn’t enjoy it on any level. Now, watching friends anticipate birth, I want what I know what I missed.
docs.lead_paragraph: It might have been the photo of the onesie with the due date circled. It might have been the confidential email I got. It might have been all the ultrasound photos, seemingly within days of one another, popping up on my Facebook feed. It might have been when one friend told me her obstetrician said she was a champ, or the day another friend talked about getting 78 pounds of maternity clothes from her best friend, some still unopened, or the latest email from the yoga place that I never go to anymore advertising the prenatal yoga class I never took. It might have been any of those things, or it might just have been the all-too-common effects of depression combined with sleep deprivation, but suddenly I broke down in tears.

headline.main: The Pregnancy I Endured, and the One I Missed

docs.snippet: Osaka, Japan’s third-largest city, is increasingly the place to taste domestic craft brews.
docs.lead_paragraph: For a long time, drinking beer in Japan meant implicitly supporting one of the country’s four major producers: Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo. But in the mid-1990s, when a law prohibiting the operation of small-scale breweries was abandoned, the door was opened for Japanese craft beer, known as ji-biru. Even today, there are only about 200 craft breweries in Japan, so finding domestic microbrews takes some effort. (For comparison, the United States had nearly 2,500 craft breweries in operation as of June 2013, according to the Brewers Association.) But increasingly, the place to taste these relatively rare — but deliciously well-crafted — beers is Osaka, Japan’s third-largest city.

headline.main: A Craft-Beer Pub Crawl in the ‘Kitchen of Japan’

Or maybe it’s that in this metropolis of eight million — with its screaming energy and melting pot of cultures — “only in the movies” events seem to happen on a daily basis. docs.abstract: Running marathons as an insight into human psychology and investor behavior.
docs.snippet: Running marathons as an insight into human psychology and investor behavior.
docs.lead_paragraph: George Wu, who is not only a keen student of the sport, but also a professor of behavioral science at the University of Chicago, spent Monday night downloading the official times of all 31,805 finishers. The distribution of finishing times follows the same pattern I highlighted in this morning’s column, with a statistically improbable clumping of runners finishing just before their goals of 3, 3.5 or 4 hours, and an accompanying “gap” with far fewer runners finishing just minutes after their goals. Befitting Boston’s reputation as a race for truly competitive runners, there’s less evidence of such goals mattering for those aiming to beat 5 or 6 hours.

headline.main: Monday’s Boston Marathon provides yet more data illustrating that arbitrary numbers can serve as motivating goals.

docs.abstract: Some thoughts on the likelihood of near-future inequality-driven upheavals.
docs.snippet: Some thoughts on the likelihood of near-future inequality-driven upheavals.
docs.lead_paragraph: My Sunday column, on Thomas Piketty’s revival of the old argument that capitalism tends to enrich the capital-rich Few much, much faster than the laboring Many, didn’t take a position on the plausibility of the French economist’s basic forecast, which foresees upper-tail inequality rising forever absent a sustained political disruption. (For a more qualified observer’s critique of that forecast, Tyler Cowen’s review and follow-up are the place to turn.) Instead, I argued against the view that such a trend would necessarily lead to such political disruptions, or indeed be particularly destabilizing to the developed world’s societies. So long as a rich country’s Many see some real gains, I suggested, whether through modest growth and/or modestly-increasing redistribution, we aren’t likely to see anything remotely like the kind of literal class warfare that the last gilded age produced.

headline.main: Piketty, Doom Loops and Haymarket

docs.lead_paragraph: The life and career of the designer Patrick Kelly were as brief as they were brilliant. Jones.

docs.lead_paragraph: KIEV, Ukraine — The word “maidan” means “square” in Ukrainian and in Arabic. And the “Independence Maidan” of Kiev, like the “Tahrir Maidan” of Cairo, has been the scene of an awe-inspiring burst of democratic aspirations. The barricades of piled cobblestones, tires, wood beams and burned cars erected by Ukrainian revolutionaries are still there — indeed, it looks as if it could be the set of “Les Misérables” — and people still lay fresh flowers at the makeshift shrines for the more than 100 people killed in the Maidan by the old and now deposed regime here. Walking through it, though, I tried to explain to my host that, while I was incredibly impressed, a lot of Americans today have “Maidan fatigue” — too many dashed hopes for democracy in too many squares — from Afghanistan to Iran, Iraq to Egypt, Syria to Libya.

But until Tuesday, their lawyers were unsure how to proceed with the appeal because the judges had never explained the reduced charge. Prosecutors had accused the Huangs of starving their daughter, Gloria, 8, and originally suspected them of being child traffickers because the defendants are of Asian heritage and the child was African. The Huangs, who attributed the child’s death to an eating disorder, said the prosecution was based on flawed evidence, racial prejudices and misunderstandings about Western adoption.

docs.lead_paragraph: India’s Supreme Court announced Tuesday that it would hear an appeal of its decision in December that re-criminalized gay sex. The hearing is largely a formality and is unlikely to lead to a serious reconsideration of the decision. A lower court ruled in 2009 that an 1861 law mandating a 10-year sentence for “carnal intercourse against the order of nature with man, woman or animal” was unconstitutional. But the Supreme Court overturned the lower court’s decision, holding that only Parliament had the power to change that law.

docs.abstract: At least two people died on Tuesday after a day of violence in a slum that abuts the Copacabana tourist district of Rio de Janeiro.
docs.snippet: At least two people died on Tuesday after a day of violence in a slum that abuts the Copacabana tourist district of Rio de Janeiro.
docs.lead_paragraph: At least two people died Tuesday after a day of violence in a slum that abuts the Copacabana tourist district of Rio de Janeiro. Local news media reported that the deaths occurred in the slum, or favela, called Pavão-Pavãozinho. The disturbances began after a young man who was a dancer on a television variety show was found dead and residents charged that he had been killed by a police officer, according to the reports. The police said that they were investigating, but that marks on the man’s body indicated that he could have fallen to his death. A protest turned violent, and several officers became trapped in the favela. An elite squad then arrived. Copacabana residents reported hearing gunshots and what sounded like small explosions. A second man was later found fatally shot. Separately, a police officer was shot in another favela in the north of the city. The violence comes less than two months before Rio and other cities in Brazil are to host the World Cup.

headline.main: Brazil: Deadly Violence Erupts in Rio
headline.print_headline: Brazil: Violence Erupts in Rio

(Starz Cinema) CHICKEN WITH PLUMS (2012) A celebrated but tormented violinist, Nasser-Ali (Mathieu Amalric, above), in 1958 Tehran retreats to his bed to end his life after his prized instrument is broken, in this drama from Marjane Satrapi and Vincent Paronnaud, based on Ms. Satrapi’s graphic novel of the same title. But in flashbacks — and flash-forwards — starring Nasser-Ali’s wife (Maria de Medeiros) and children (Mathis Bour and Enna Balland; Chiara Mastroianni and Christian Friedel portray them as adults), it soon becomes clear that his melancholy is rooted in a deeper heartache: his long-ago love, Irane (Golshifteh Farahani). “Not that ‘Chicken With Plums’ is gloomy,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times. “Like its swooning, madly melodramatic musical score (by Olivier Bernet), the film takes an almost giddy pleasure in unhappiness, turning even pedestrian moments of boredom or discomfort into occasions for wild invention.” The result, which features a naked Sophia Loren and Edouard Baer as the Angel of Death, “is captivating, but not exactly moving.”
